name: Liam Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a drinks distributor's warehouse by the canal, the place that supplies pubs, restaurants and corner shops. I start at five in the morning. I pick cases of beer, cola and bottled water onto pallets for each delivery run, and shrink-wrap them for the drivers. Kegs are the heaviest bit, and I'm still learning to roll them without wrecking my wrists.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The early start wears me out, and the cold in the keg store. I like that by one o'clock I'm done, and on Sundays I help my dad in his corner shop. My girlfriend Priya works at a nursery looking after toddlers. We're saving to get engaged properly, ring and all, but saving is a big word for what we manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a bit of common sense at last. Work is work, people should do it. At the shop, Dad would say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it means I keep my job. But it doesn't fix the pay, which is low because I'm new and slow. The real stress is money, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, try to get faster on the picks so I can go up a pay band. I'd keep using the AI app now and then for Dad's stock orders, because he can't work it. And I'd try to put 30 a month away for the ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit stuck. Like I'm running on the spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said saving is a big word. What do you actually manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 20 a month, some months nothing. Priya puts in more than me, which I don't love. My dad always paid for everything at home, and I'd like to be that for my girlfriend Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says it's honest work and I should learn a trade on top. He wanted me to be an electrician, like his cousin. I didn't finish school, so I put it off.

say: Good, a bit of **common sense** at last.
**Work is work**, and people should do it, as Dad would say in the shop.
think: I keep my job, but the **pay stays low** because I'm new and slow.
The real stress is **money**, not machines.
do: Get faster on picks to reach the next **pay band**.
Put **30 a month** away for an engagement ring.
Keep using the **AI app** for Dad's stock orders.
feel: **Steady but stuck**, like running on the spot.

fieldNote: His job feels **safe**, but he saves only about 20 a month.
He holds a **traditional provider** ideal and dislikes Priya paying more.
He uses **AI occasionally**, mainly to help his father's shop.

steps.text: Speed up keg and case picking to reach the next pay band
Put 30 a month aside for an engagement ring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and we'll get through it like we always do. People should learn a trade, not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's probably safe for a few years, because rolling kegs isn't something a robot does well yet. But the office side, ordering and routes, would go to software. If the company gets leaner, they might stop the overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking, and once a couple of mates had done it, I'd sign up for the electrician apprenticeship evening course. I'd keep saving, even if it means fewer nights out. Maybe use AI tools for the course theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's a push I probably needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything already changing at the drinks warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The new route planner at the drinks warehouse cut one driver run a week already. The drivers moan about it every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the electrician course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if Steve from my shift came too. He's been talking about it. Doing it with someone makes it easier.

say: It's change, and we'll **get through it** like we always do.
People should learn a **trade**, not wait for handouts.
think: Rolling **kegs** isn't something robots do well yet, so I'm safe for a few years.
Office work like **ordering and routes** goes to software first.
do: Sign up for an **electrician evening course** once mates have done it.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, with a push I probably needed.
S1.quote: The new route planner at the drinks warehouse cut one driver run a week already.
fieldNote: He's already seen **route software** cut a driver run.

steps.text: Start an electrician evening course alongside Steve from his shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and companies should give people time to adjust. But I wouldn't want handouts, I'd want proper apprenticeships, paid by the firms making the money. That's what I'd say at the shop counter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means picking is gone by about 2031, so I'd have maybe three years. The thinking side, like orders and routes, goes first in 2028, and that's not my bit. If I'm not trained by 2031, I'm in Dad's shop, which barely pays him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician course straight away, no waiting for mates this time. I'd work every shift they give me and save everything that's left, even if it's only 50. Priya and I would put the ring off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops, like missing a step on the stairs in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots around 2031. What do you do in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study like mad, evenings and weekends, while the job's still paying. Dad would cover my Sundays at the shop so I could do coursework. I'd keep rolling kegs every morning until the day they don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya about the ring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the ring waits, but I'm not going anywhere. She'd understand, she's the sensible one. I'd still feel like I'd let her down.

fieldNote: Short time pushes him to **act alone**, not wait for mates.
His fallback is **his father's shop**, which he knows barely pays.
He'd **delay the engagement** and feel he'd let Priya down.

steps.text: Start an electrician course immediately, evenings and weekends
Work every shift and save all spare money
Put off buying Priya's engagement ring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get a trade, so get one. Don't sit around waiting for someone to sort it for you. I'd tell the younger lads on the early shift the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Picking goes around 2034, so I'd have time to finish an apprenticeship and work a few years as an electrician first. That's a plan I can see. The worry is the money while I'm studying, because there's nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician course in the first year with Steve, save 40 a month, and keep picking until I qualify. Then switch to an electrical firm as an improver. I'd use the AI tools for the theory once Steve showed me how he uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I believe in. Like the start of a long shift when you know the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you still put off the ring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd get engaged, just a cheaper ring. Life goes on, and I'm not waiting on robots to marry Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say finally. He's been telling me to do electrics since I was sixteen.

I'd tell the younger lads on the **early shift** not to sit around waiting.
think: Picking goes around **2034**, enough time to finish an apprenticeship.
The worry is **money while studying**, because there's nothing spare.
do: Start the **electrician course** in year one with Steve.
Keep picking until I **qualify**, then switch.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan I believe in.
S3.quote: We'd get engaged, just a cheaper ring. Life goes on, and I'm not waiting on robots to marry Priya.
fieldNote: With five years, he keeps **family plans** with a cheaper ring.
His **apprenticeship plan** feels achievable, but money while studying worries him.
His father's long push gives this a **family story**.

steps.text: Start the electrician course in year one with Steve
Save 40 a month from picking pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plenty of time, so learn a trade and do it properly. Don't rush it, but don't waste the decade either. That's what Dad would say, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd want to be a qualified electrician with a few years behind me. Thinking AI wouldn't touch picking much, and the robots come late. I'd be fine, I think, as long as I actually start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, get faster on picks for the better pay band. Next year, start the course. Save every month, and get engaged, married, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly just getting on with life. It's on my mind on the drive in, not at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is the electrician route still the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Electricians will be needed longer than pickers, I reckon. Someone has to wire the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Priya's nursery job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's safer than mine. People want a person looking after their kids, not a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years isn't long enough to qualify and save. What would help is an apprenticeship that pays a wage while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family businesses. Dad's shop is a fallback for us, and lots of people have one.

headlineQuote: Dad's shop is a fallback for us, and lots of people have one.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old picker** at a drinks warehouse, starting at five and learning to roll kegs.
He saves about **20 a month** with his girlfriend Priya, a nursery worker, and hopes to propose.
He's **traditional and steady**, wanting a trade, not handouts, and moving once others do.
His **electrician** plan, pushed by his dad, becomes concrete across all five scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with too little time to qualify and save.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** with a wage while he learns.
